subtype: Approach: setting a goal with an amount and date [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday
Found the bicycle I want: a secondhand geared one at the repair shop near the market, 4,000 rupees. Babu Uncle at the shop says he can keep it aside for a while if I pay a little first.
First reaction: impossible. My allowance is 250 a week, and 4,000 sounds like a mountain.
But then I did the maths properly on the back of my notebook. Six months is about 26 weeks. 4,000 divided by 26 is roughly 154. Call it 160 a week, to be safe. That leaves 90 a week for everything else.
Ninety is tight but not terrible: no more samosas every day, maybe twice a week. Himani said I can come to her place for cricket instead of the gaming parlour.
So it's not a mountain. It's 160 rupees, 26 times.
Starting this Monday. Target: 12 October.
– Yusuf

qa.a: 160 a week, to be safe.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel before and after doing the maths?
qa.a: Yusuf felt it was impossible, like a mountain, then relieved and hopeful once it became 160 rupees a week.

qa.q: What else could Yusuf do if 90 a week feels too tight?
qa.a: Talk it over with a parent, and perhaps move the target date a little later so the weekly amount is gentler.

qa.q: How might Himani see the new plan?
qa.a: Himani seems supportive, offering cricket at home as a free alternative to the gaming parlour.

grounding: Shows a teen turning a 4,000-rupee bicycle goal over six months into a weekly saving figure and finding it more realistic than feared.

subtype: Approach: paying yourself first [Action]

Dear Pradeep Anna,
You asked how I finally saved for the cricket bat when I never could before. It's the trick you told me about, and it actually worked.
Before, I used to spend first and save whatever was left at the end of the month. There was never anything left. Not once.
So in January I changed the order. Appa gives me my allowance on the first Sunday of the month. That same afternoon, before I even go to the shop, I put a fixed part of it into a brown envelope marked BAT and hand the envelope to Amma to keep in her cupboard. Only then do I spend the rest.
The first month it felt like I had less money. By the third month I didn't notice. By May the envelope had enough, and Appa took me to the sports shop.
I'm keeping the envelope. Now it says BOOKS.
Karthik

qa.a: To Amma, to keep in her cupboard.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel about the new order at first, and later?
qa.a: Karthik felt short of money at first, but by the third month didn't notice, and felt proud when the bat was bought.

qa.a: Asking Appa or Amma whether a savings account would be a better place than an envelope.

qa.q: How might Pradeep Anna feel reading this letter?

subtype: Approach: paying yourself first [Action]

Ujjwal, you asked how I saved enough for the school trip to Rishikesh. I'm Vandana, and I'll tell you, because it's embarrassingly simple.
For a whole year I tried to save what was left over. You know how that goes. Nothing's ever left over. There's always a samosa, a pen, a recharge.
Then Papa helped me open a small student savings account at the bank near our school. And we made a deal: on the day my pocket money arrives, the first thing I do, before anything else, is put a fixed part into that account. At first I did it at the bank counter; now Papa helps me do it on his phone the same evening.
The rest is mine to spend, no guilt. If it runs out on the twentieth, it runs out.
It took me eight months. But in the end I didn't have to ask anyone for the trip money. That felt amazing, honestly.

subtype: Approach: tracking spending and finding leaks [Action]
passage:
I'm Neelam. Payal and I share a desk, and for the whole of July she carried a tiny notebook in her pencil box. Every time she bought anything, she wrote it down: date, what, how much. Samosa, 15. Pen, 10. Recharge, 49. Chips, 20. It seemed a bit much to me.
On the first of August she showed me the totals, grouped by type. Snacks and phone top-ups together were a third of everything she had spent. She looked honestly surprised.
She didn't do anything dramatic. She said she'd keep one canteen snack on Fridays and bring fruit from home on other days, and she switched to a cheaper recharge pack her brother told her about. She still bought stickers when she wanted them.
By the end of August her notebook had a new line at the bottom: saved. I don't know exactly how much. But she was smiling when she wrote it.

qa.q: How much did a recharge cost in Payal's notebook?
qa.a: Recharge, 49.

qa.q: How did Payal feel on seeing the totals on the first of August?
qa.a: Payal looked honestly surprised to see that snacks and top-ups took a third of her spending.

qa.q: Why did trimming only snacks and top-ups work better than cutting everything?
qa.a: It targeted the two biggest leaks while leaving room for small joys like stickers, so the change was easy to keep.

qa.q: How does Payal's month look to Neelam?
qa.a: Neelam first thought the notebook was a bit much, then saw it lead to a real, cheerful change.

Mid-March, a Saturday: The notebook is filling up. Momos with friends, 40. Recharge, 99. Cold drink, 20. Another recharge, 49, because the data ran out. Seema is annoyed at how often “momos” and “recharge” appear.

30 April: For the first time, she still has money left on the thirtieth.

Abhinav got 9 out of 10 on his tables test today and did a little dance.
Plan for the money: half into my laptop jar, which I've been filling from pocket money since January, and the rest is mine. With the tutoring, the jar should fill by Diwali instead of next summer.

subtype: Approach: spending impulsively at the first temptation [Pitfall]
passage:
Last March I had 2,600 rupees saved toward a secondhand bicycle. I'm Sumit. I'd been putting away 150 a week since October, and the cycle was 4,000, so I was about nine weeks away.
Then one night a sale popped up on my phone: white sneakers, “ends in 2 hours”, 1,200 rupees, down from 2,500. Harish had the same pair. I didn't think. I asked Mummy to pay with her card and gave her the cash from my tin the next morning. It felt amazing for about a day.
Then I did the maths. 2,600 minus 1,200 left 1,400. I now needed 2,600 more instead of 1,400. At 150 a week, that pushed the cycle back by about two months. The summer I'd planned to ride to the lake became a summer of walking.
The shoes are nice. But every time I tie them, I think: that's two months.

qa.q: How much did the sneakers cost in the sale?
qa.a: 1,200 rupees, down from 2,500.

qa.q: How does Sumit feel now when tying the shoes?
qa.a: Sumit feels a pang of regret, remembering the two months the cycle was pushed back.

qa.q: What could Sumit have done when the two-hour sale popped up?
qa.a: Wait until morning and check the goal first, or talk it over with Mummy, since a short timer is designed to rush decisions.

qa.q: How might Harish see Sumit buying the same pair?
qa.a: Harish might be flattered or not notice at all, unaware that matching the shoes cost Sumit two months of saving.

grounding: Shows a teen buying sneakers on impulse in an online sale, which sets the bicycle goal back by about two months.

Parent's note, kept with Ira's savings chart
Ira has been saving for a bicycle since the summer, and I have watched her tick her chart every Sunday. By last week she was a little over halfway.
On Tuesday evening she came to me with her phone, excited. A sale on a shopping site: sports shoes at almost half price, “today only”. She asked me to pay by card from her savings, and I did, because it was her money and her decision. Her sister Damini said the shoes were lovely.
On Sunday she sat with the chart and worked it out herself. At her weekly amount, the shoes had pushed the bicycle back by about two months, past her birthday. She went quiet for a while. Then she said, “The shoes were a today-only feeling. The bicycle is an every-day thing.”
I did not lecture. I think she learned more from her own chart than she would have from me.

In Class Nine I spent most of my allowance on things I didn't even like. I'm Dhruv, and I can explain.
My group ate lunch at the canteen, and they always ordered the expensive stuff: cold coffee, cheese sandwiches, the big chocolate bar. My tiffin from home suddenly looked babyish. So I ordered what they ordered. Cold coffee, which I don't really like. Every day.
Once Minakshi from our class said she'd rather save for the science fair kit, and one of the boys laughed, and I laughed too, though I secretly wanted that kit as well.
At the end of the month I emptied my wallet on my bed. Sixty rupees. I'd wanted a set of drawing pens for months, and now it was months away again.
The worst part was that nobody would have noticed if I'd opened my tiffin. I was paying not to feel left out, and I still felt it.

qa.a: Sixty rupees.

Parent's note, end of the month
Gautam asked me today for an advance on next month's allowance, the second time this term. When I asked what for, it turned out to be the model rocket kit he has talked about since summer. He had planned to buy it with this month's money.
We sat down and went through where the money went. Almost all of it had gone at the café near his tuition, where his friends go after class: milkshakes, fries, sometimes pizza on Fridays. He admitted he often wasn't hungry. “If I just sit there with nothing, it's weird,” he said. His cousin Binita, who goes to the same tuition, said most of them feel the same and nobody says so.
He was quiet and a bit ashamed. I did not give the advance. We agreed he would try going to the café only on Fridays and see how it feels. I will check with him at the end of next month.

The thermometer is still on my wall, even though the camera was bought long ago. I'm Kalyani, and I drew it the day I decided to save for a secondhand camera: a tall red bulb on chart paper, with lines from zero at the bottom to the full amount at the top, one line for each week's saving.
Every Sunday night I coloured one line red. That was it. But it worked in a way I didn't expect. In weeks when everyone was going to the new ice-cream place, or when Irawati wanted to go to the mall, I'd look at the half-red thermometer and think, I don't want an empty line this week. Sometimes I went anyway and just had water. Twice I skipped.
Around week fifteen the red passed the halfway mark, and I actually cheered. By week twenty-eight the red touched the top.
Irawati says it's childish. She's drawing one now too.

qa.a: Coloured one line red.

Class teacher's note, money-skills project, week twelve
When the class began the saving project, most students kept their totals in a notebook and forgot about them. Kiran did something different. She drew a large thermometer on chart paper and taped it inside her locker door, with the goal, a set of watercolours and brushes, written at the top.
Every Monday she coloured in the week's saving. I noticed that in the weeks after the school fête and the book fair, when others spent everything, her thermometer still went up, just by a smaller amount. When I asked how, she said, “I didn't want a gap in it. It looks sad.”
Her younger sister Yamini, in Class Six, has started coming to the locker to see it.
This week the red reached the top. Kiran showed me the paints before assembly. I will ask her to share the idea with the class.

subtype: Approach: falling for easy-money schemes online [Pitfall]

Parent's note, Thursday night
This evening Vijay came to me with his phone and his savings tin. A video had promised that money put into a “game app” today would double in a week, “guaranteed”. It showed a boy his age holding up a new phone. Vijay had already typed his savings amount into the app's payment page and wanted my card to finish it.
He was excited in a way I recognised: he had already spent the doubled money in his head. His friend Sarika had forwarded the same link and was about to pay too.
I asked him to sit with me before pressing anything. We looked up the app's name together and found many complaints. I explained that anything promising to double money quickly is almost always a fraud, and that real saving is slow. He was quiet, then disappointed, then relieved.
We deleted the app. He messaged Sarika at once: “Don't pay. It's a scam. Ask your mum."

qa.q: What did the video promise?
qa.a: That money put into a game app today would double in a week, guaranteed.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel as the conversation went on?
qa.a: Vijay was excited at first, then quiet and disappointed, and finally relieved.

qa.q: What could Vijay do the next time such an offer appears?
qa.a: Pause and show a parent before paying, and look up complaints, since quick-doubling promises are usually frauds.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel getting Vijay's message?
qa.a: Sarika may feel startled and a bit embarrassed, but relieved to be warned before paying.

grounding: A parent notes a teen nearly sending savings to a double-your-money game app before the parent explains that such offers are usually frauds.

Nearly did something really dumb today.
Divyansh showed me an ad inside a game: “Invest your pocket money, get double in 7 days. 100% safe.” There were screenshots of people's payments, all green ticks. I have 1,800 saved for a football. Double would be 3,600. I started picturing the boots too.
I went to Baba to ask for help paying on his phone, trying to make it sound small. He read the ad for about ten seconds and put the phone face down.
He said, “Arnab, if a stranger could double money in seven days, why would they need your 1,800?” Then he showed me a news report about the same kind of app, where children lost everything they put in.
I felt stupid, then angry at the ad, then just glad. I texted Divyansh not to do it either.
The football still costs what it costs. Six more weeks.

Zeenat's target was a secondhand tablet for her drawing, with a goal date of 15 December and a fixed weekly amount. Through August and September she hit every week.
Then October happened: a school trip fee, a new geometry box after hers was lost, and a costume for annual day. She had to use some of the saved money, and three weeks' saving went into these instead.
At the check-in she looked frustrated. Her classmate Joseph, whose plan had also slipped, said he was going to give up. Zeenat didn't. She redid the numbers in front of me: move the date four weeks later, to 12 January, and save a slightly smaller amount each week, which she said felt “doable, not punishing”.

Bad month for the savings plan. The goal was a pair of football boots by 30 November, saving the same amount every week. Then school asked for a lab manual, a new tie (mine tore), and money for the Children's Day class party. My jar went down instead of up.
My first thought was to give up. I told Farhan, and he said, “Just forget the boots, man.”
But tonight I sat down and looked at it properly. The boots aren't gone. The date is just wrong now. If I move it four weeks, to 28 December, I can save a bit less each week and still get there. A smaller number I'll actually manage beats a bigger one I'll quit.
I rewrote the plan on a fresh page and showed Ammi. She said it looked sensible.
New date: 28 December.
– Vijay

subtype: Approach: splitting money into save, spend and give [Thinking]

Thomas, you asked why I keep three jars on my shelf, even now. It started when I was fourteen.
My father gave me pocket money every Sunday, and I felt pulled three ways. I wanted a sewing machine, badly. I also wanted chaat with friends. And every month the mosque collected for flood families, and I felt bad putting in nothing.
So one Sunday I sat on my bed and thought it through. The machine mattered most, so half would go to that. Fun mattered too, so a third was mine to spend without guilt. And what was left, the smallest part, was for giving: Ammi's birthday, the flood box. My mother said, “Dilnaz, you've made it fair to everyone, including yourself.”
It took a year to buy the machine. But I never felt mean, or guilty, or deprived.
So your jars can be different sizes, Thomas. Just make sure all three exist.

qa.q: What did the smallest part go toward?
qa.a: Giving: Ammi's birthday and the flood box.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel before making the split?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt pulled three ways and guilty about giving nothing to the flood families.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the plan feel fair?
qa.a: Deciding a share for each want and value, the machine, fun and giving, instead of letting one crowd out the others.

subtype: Approach: splitting money into save, spend and give [Thinking]
passage:
Madhuri's allowance had shrunk that year. The family's tailoring shop had a slow season, and Nirmala Aunty, who ran it with Madhuri's mother, said everyone was tightening. So when Madhuri got her small weekly amount, every rupee felt like it had three jobs to do.
She sat at the shop counter after closing and thought aloud to her aunt. “I want the art course in summer. That's the big one, so half goes there. I don't want to be the only one who never buys a samosa, so about a third is for me. And the rest... Diwali gifts for you and Amma, and a little for the temple's food drive.”
Nirmala Aunty raised an eyebrow. “Even the giving, when money's tight?”
“Especially when it's tight,” Madhuri said. “Otherwise it feels like money only ever goes one way.”
She wrote labels on three envelopes and tucked them under the counter drawer.

qa.q: How much of the allowance goes to the art course?
qa.a: Half goes there.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri keep a share for giving even when money was tight?
qa.a: She felt it mattered to her values, not wanting to feel that money only ever went one way.

qa.q: What else could Madhuri do if the slow season continues?
qa.a: Talk with Amma and Nirmala Aunty about adjusting the shares or the course date, rather than dropping the plan.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty see Madhuri's answer?
qa.a: Nirmala Aunty may be surprised and touched that Madhuri keeps room for giving in a hard year.
